reason: The court adopted the co-owner prescription principle in its reasoning, but the supporting quote is expressly from Tillekeratne v. Bastian rather than this court's own holding.
The minority and absence point came from an earlier case used only by analogy under section 13, while this appeal turned on section 3 and tacking after discounting the life-interest period.
The quoted sentence is this court's own reason for ordering the interim injunction and accurately states that quantifiable damages alone is not a sufficient refusal ground.
The statement reflects the section 25 partition-duty reasoning, but the quoted passage is a quotation from Juliana Hamine rather than this court's own formulation.
The rule is part of the holding on revision, but the selected quote only supports statutory-disregard as exceptional circumstances and omits the failure-to-appeal aspect.
The court itself held that the plaintiff had not proved title and stated the burden rule as the basis for dismissing the declaration-of-title appeal.
The quoted passage is this court's own section 70 reasoning on non-prosecution in partition actions and supports the dismissal of the appeal.
The court itself applied section 83 of the Trusts Ordinance and the bona fide purchaser point to restore the District Court's declaration of ownership.
The mortgage-security principle was adopted in affirming the injunction, but the selected quote is from Halsbury rather than this court's own holding.
The substitution rule is this court's holding, but the non-empty statute field names only the Civil Procedure Code generally and not the actual substituted provision construed.
The court rejected the section 31 Notaries Ordinance attack on the mortgage bonds and treated non-compliance as not vitiating the documents.
The court itself stated, under proviso (1) to section 92 of the Evidence Ordinance, that evidence aliunde could be led on consideration before rejecting the claim on proof.
The court applied section 8 of the Prescription Ordinance to goods-sold-and-delivered documents and held the claim prescribed after one year.
The sentence reflects the evidentiary finding in this dispute, but it is a fact-specific inference about the fixed asset register rather than a legal ratio.
The court held that section 8 did not apply because the vessel was not sold and delivered, while the statement miscasts the one-year limitation as a delivery requirement.
The court applied section 7 of the Prescription Ordinance to an unwritten overdraft agreement and held the three-year period ran from default.
The suretyship holding is supported by this court's own conclusion, but the cited statute field points to Evidence Ordinance section 101, which was not the provision construed.
The extracted wording is an incomplete textbook example from Prof. Weeramantry, not this court's operative holding about the parties' correspondence forming a written contract.
The court itself placed the burden on the judgment debtor under section 763 to prove substantial loss and dismissed the challenge to the writ order.
The court answered the agreed issue in those words, but the statement omits the material Cabinet-approval basis and the statute field is an unrelated fragmentation-law provision.
The six-year written-contract point was discussed only for completeness after the defendant did not pursue prescription, so it is not a ratio of this appeal.
The court used the company-name-change principle as part of its analysis of continuing corporate rights and liabilities in the appeal.
The demand-loan rule was applied to reject prescription, but the cited Civil Procedure Code section 40(d) was not the provision construed for that rule.
The court applied the section 170 damages principles to reduce the award to loss proved by the two actionable telecasts.
The court held that the defendant waived its jurisdiction objection by not taking it as a preliminary issue under section 147 and by participating in the trial.
